records.proposal: T1 Wild Privet (Ligustrum vulgare) Front garden boundary, directly wedged between the masonry front boundary wall and active underground drainage infrastructure. Fell to near ground level and chemically treat/grind stump to prevent vigorous basal and epicormic re-sprouting. Compromised Health & Poor Historic Tree Care: T1 exhibits poor physiological and structural condition following heavy, substandard heading cuts and blunt lopping carried out under previous ownership. This improper pruning has disrupted the natural canopy habit, resulting in dense, erratic epicormic water shoots with weak basal and branch attachments that are prone to tearing. Several historical flush cuts have failed to occlude properly, leaving exposed deadwood and areas of localized internal decay. The specimen cannot be pruned back to a balanced, viable, or structurally sound form. T2 Species: Holly (Ilex aquifolium) Front garden (marked as T2) Dismantle and fell 1no. Holly tree to ground level and replace with 1no. high-quality Magnolia specimen tree in an unconstrained location within the front garden. Comparison with Pruned Precedent vs. High-Value Replacement: A comparable Holly tree on the immediate neighbouring property has previously undergone heavy pruning/reduction to manage boundary conflicts. The resulting appearance is austere, unnatural, and visually discordant, highlighting how poorly mature Holly responds aesthetically to severe containment pruning. Applying a similar harsh pruning regime to T2 would significantly degrade the visual amenity of the front curtilage and street scene. Replacing the tree entirely with an ornamental Magnolia represents a vastly superior arboricultural and visual outcome compared to maintaining a harshly reduced, mutilated Holly. records.proposal: TPO005 T1 & T2 - 2 Lime (Tilia spp.) - Re-pollard both trees back to the established previous pruning points, removing approximately 1.5-2.0m of the current regrowth from the height and lateral spread, subject to the location of the historic pollard heads. Retain the existing pollard framework and avoid cutting beyond the established previous reduction points. Crown lift both trees to provide approximately 2.5m clearance above the adjoining pedestrian footpath, by selectively removing or shortening low secondary branches only. Remove any dead, damaged or crossing branches encountered during the works. Reason: Routine management of previously pollarded Lime trees; to contain crown dimensions, maintain the established pruning regime and provide suitable clearance above the adjoining pedestrian footpath. T3 - Horse Chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum) Crown reduce the tree by approximately 2.0-2.5m from the height and lateral spread, pruning back to suitable secondary growth points and maintaining a balanced, natural crown form. The finished crown dimensions should be approximately 4-5m smaller in overall diameter than existing. Crown thin by up to 20%, concentrating on selective removal of secondary growth throughout the crown without creating excessive internal voids or removing significant structural limbs. Crown lift to provide approximately 4.0m clearance above ground level, through selective removal or shortening of lower secondary branches. Remove all deadwood throughout the crown. Reason: General crown management to reduce overall crown dimensions and end-weight, improve crown structure and maintain appropriate clearance beneath the tree.

records.proposal: TPO225 TG1 - Large Conifer Group - Located in rear garden - to fell. Reason - The conifer group has become significantly overgrown and is causing concerns for the neighbouring property due to its size and resulting loss of light. The trees also generate ongoing debris and bird-related fouling, resulting in a persistent nuisance to the neighbouring garden. Felling is proposed to address these concerns and allow the garden to be maintained more effectively. T1 - Lime - Located in rear garden - Would like to crown reduce removing up to 3m. Reason - The tree has become large in relation to the garden and is causing concerns for the neighbouring property, particularly regarding loss of light and the overhang of the crown. The tree also produces significant quantities of seeds, which fall into the neighbouring garden. A crown reduction of up to 3m is proposed to reduce the overall size and spread of the tree whilst retaining it as a suitable and sustainable landscape feature.
